update.notes: Mark places the Hendee Home at 304 West Hurst. The 1909 numbering puts the 300s on the block from Jackson to Washington, and this is the house already on the Hurst end of that block, Barnes side. Which side of Hurst took the even numbers was not found, so the side is an estimate. February 1912 is the first sheet that draws these lots. No year-built was found in the assessor file. The Italianate front, belvedere, and stacked porch are from the photograph. The label is Hendee Home. The 1885 history names S. A. Hendee and J. W. Hendee and does not say which of them lived here.

Block 59 is Hurst to Hail, East Main to Crafford. The February 1912 and earlier sheets were read for that block. W. J. add.notes: photo from Mark, 292 W Hurst St, 2010. The 1909 numbering puts 300 at Jackson on West Hurst and 304 on the Barnes side of the Jackson–Washington block, which is where the Hendee Home stands. 292 is the even number just Dean-side of Jackson, on that same Barnes side. February 1912 sheet 3 is the first sheet that draws block 70, Barnes to Hurst, Dean to Jackson, and it shows dwellings there, but no lot on that sheet was matched to the number 292, so the footprint is an estimate from the photograph, about 40 by 42 feet. The brick first story, the round brick porch with white columns and steps, the blue-gray slate mansard, the red eaves, the pedimented dormer, and the front gable with the arched window are the photograph. No family name is printed. The start year is an estimate. The house stays through 1970. survivesTo 2010 records that it was standing for the photograph. The stand-in on this corner, house-147, comes off from the 1910 stop.

add.name: East Side School

facade.photoSource: Mark's photograph of the high school on Cole Street.

facadeSpec.citation: Mark's photograph of the high school on Cole Street
estimates: The Sanborn sheets were not read for a separate school lot.

add.notes: The 1875–76 East Side school at Cole and Hurst burned in 1896. The centennial book says the East Side school opened in the winter of 1904. This is that building, on the same corner: three stories of red brick, a hipped roof, and the corner tower with the arched entry and open belfry in Mark's photograph. It replaces the 1875 school, which comes off at the 1900 stop because the May 1898 map is after the fire. The new school appears at the 1910 stop, the first stop after the winter of 1904. Mark says it was torn down in the late 1980s, after 1970, so it stays through the last year drawn. The Sanborn sheets were not read for a separate school lot.

facadeSpec.citation: Mark's photograph of the C. S. Norcross building, about 2020
estimates: The steel bins in the photograph are not dated before 1970, so they are not drawn.

add.notes: The centennial book says C. S. Norcross and Sons let the contract for their building in May 1906, and that it is the concrete-block factory at the corner of Davis and Dean, still in use when the book was written. A later line says he moved the factory to Bushnell in 1903. The 1906 contract is the date used for this block building. It is drawn from the 1910 stop, the first stop after May 1906. The 1954 directory still lists C. S. Norcross & Sons at Dean and Davis. Mark says the building was torn down in 2026. The model stops at 1970, so that demolition is recorded and not drawn. The rock-faced walls use the stone texture, because the model has no separate concrete-block material. The steel bins and the metal building in the about-2020 photograph are not dated before 1970, so they are not drawn.

add.notes: Location per Mark Rauschert, Nov 2026: the 500 block of East Main, south of the 60-foot Ball Bros. front, not against that facade. No Sanborn engine-house or hose-house label was read on this block, so the year is an estimate and the tower is drawn from the 1910 stop, the postcard's era.
